Pour les verbes, la règle de réalisation est plus complexe, et nécessite des données supplémentaires, notamment textuelles. new_statements.translation: For nouns, the accent is always on the last syllable of the lexical root. For verbs, the realisation rule is more complex and requires additional data, especially textual data. It seems that the accent can be distinctive in some cases, as in the minimal pair ipyáka 'arms (pl.)' ~ ípyaka 'I know'. Valenzuela's (1995) alphabet did not provide for writing it, but it was revised by the Chiquitanos themselves; it is now marked with an acute accent.
new_statements.citation: Sans, Pierric. 2010. Éléments de sociolinguistique et de phonologie du bésɨro (chiquitano), langue en danger des basses terres de Bolivie. Mémoire de Master 2 (dir. Colette Grinevald), Université Lumière Lyon 2. 203 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapitre 4 'Phonologie suprasegmentale', §4.4.1 'Remarques générales', subsection 'Accent', p. 110 (PDF p. 130); minimal pair also cited p. 42
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (203 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the author Pierric Sans, LaTeX 2010; downloaded from the open DDL-CNRS fulltext server). Rendered PDF page 130 (printed p. 110, running head "CHAPITRE 4 : Phonologie suprasegmentale") and checked it against the page image: under the bold sub-heading "Accent" inside §4.4 "Le mot" / §4.4.1 "Remarques générales" the passage reads exactly as quoted: "Pour les noms, l'accent est toujours dans la dernière syllabe de la racine lexicale. Pour les verbes, la règle de réalisation est plus complexe, et nécessite des données supplémentaires, notamment textuelles. Il semble que l'accent puisse être distinctif dans certains cas, comme dans la paire minimale ipyáka…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In nouns, primary stress falls on the final syllable of the lexical root (i.e. stress is anchored to the root edge, before the obligatory nominal suffix -xɨ/-ʂ/-s and before person inflection); in verbs the placement is more complex and left undescribed; stress can be contrastive (minimal pairs exist). Other first-hand sources on the same language disagree in emphasis: Krüsi & Krüsi 1978:87 (Lomerío) say stress 'depends on grammatical forms', moves with affixes, and shows 'no regularity as to on which syllable the stress will go in stems or whole words'; Ciucci & Macoñó Tomichá 2018:48-49 (San Ignacio de Velasco) say stress is phonologically contrastive, may shift with prosodic context, and that 3rd-person possessive suffixes fix it on the final (-x, sg./pl. non-masc.) or penultimate (-ma, 3pl masc.) syllable; Santana 2012:189-191 (Brazilian Chiquitano) counts stress as non-contrastive and mostly penultimate (but final in 67% of disyllables). Nikulin 2022 (Migueleño, sanm1288) shows stress is lexically specified per morpheme and determined by the last suffix(es), within the last three syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Sans 2010, Krüsi & Krüsi 1978 or Ciucci & Macoñó 2018. Santana 2012:189 uses only 'culminância' (one main stress per word) and says syllable weight/duration were not considered. Nikulin 2022:6 fn.3, 24 (Migueleño) finds two lexemes with possible extra prominence but judges the evidence insufficient for contrastive secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Sans: verbs do not follow the noun rule and need further study; he lists 'la place de l’accent dans le mot' as an unresolved point (p. 173, conclusion). Krüsi & Krüsi: some affixes always take stress (-ti 'he'), others never (-ma 'they'); minimal pairs /'aka/ 'you are' vs /a'ka/ 'carry!' are rare. Ciucci & Macoñó: accent position can change in the same word form depending on prosodic context; dropping of -x before a possessor noun shifts stress (sapatúx → sapátu Torórixh). Riester 1967-68:178 (older Concepción/Lomerío data) gives orthographic rules: final stress in words ending in r, s, y ('bastantes excepciones'), penultimate in vowel-final words, otherwise written accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word in citation/elicited forms and wordlist items; Sans's data are elicited lexical items with numbered wordlist references). Sans notes the root-final noun stress relative to the obligatory nominal suffix; Ciucci & Macoñó note phrase-level shifts when a possessor noun follows. Nikulin 2022 describes a syntactically conditioned rightward shift in content questions for Migueleño only.
new_statements.identity_note: Sans 2010 describes the bésɨro of Lomerío (San Antonio de Lomerío, Ñuflo de Chávez province) = the 'Lomeriano' member of chiq1248; Krüsi & Krüsi 1978 also Lomerío (their text sample is from San Antonio de Lomerío, 1970). Ciucci & Macoñó Tomichá 2018 describe the San Ignacio de Velasco ('Ignaciano') dialect, the other member of chiq1248 (Glottolog dialect 'San Ignacio de Velazco Chiquitano'). Santana 2012 describes Brazilian Chiquitano (Vila Nova Barbecho, Acorizal, Central, Fazendinha; Porto Esperidião, Mato Grosso), which Glottolog folds into chiq1248 (countries BO;BR). Nikulin 2022 (the only detailed stress study) is on Migueleño Chiquitano, which Nikulin himself and Glottolog 5.1 treat as a separate language, sanm1288 — already held in our catalog; it is NOT the statement for chiq1248, though Nikulin (2022:1-2, 6) says its analysis may extend to all dialects and that stress is contrastive and paradigm-mobile in bésɨro too.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 87 (verified on page image): 'Stress in Chiquitano depends on grammatical forms. It moves about in a word according to what affixes the word takes. Some affixes will always take the stress, e.g. -ti 'he' and some will never take it e.g. -ma 'they'.. There is no regularity as to on which syllable the stress will go in stems or whole words.' Examples 'nitanu 'my head' vs ni'pakü 'my mother'; few minimal pairs (/'aka/ 'you are' vs /a'ka/ 'carry!'); stress not. Only pp. 86-93 of the 41-page paper are in the excerpt; the main suprasegmental chapter (II.5) is not held by the project.

sources.note: Migueleño (Glottolog sanm1288, a separate language already in our catalog): 'acento libre y móvil'; stress falls on one of the last three syllables, is lexically unpredictable in unsuffixed words but stable within prefixal paradigms, and in suffixed words is determined by the underlying accentual property of the last suffix(es) (pp. 6-8); alternative metric analysis: right-edge trochee with diacritic accents/extrametricality (p. 24); rightward shift to final syllable in content questions (§5). pp. 1-2 review the other dialects: stress is contrastive and paradigm-mobile in bésɨro (citing Sans…

sources.note: p. 178 'EL ACENTO': 'Existe una cierta regularidad de acentuación': (1) final stress (unwritten) in words ending in r, s (z), y, e.g. čapaor, komones, kises ('hay bastantes excepciones'); (2) penultimate if the vowel-final word has no other accent (ãsamuka, poñi); (3) all other words get a written accent (tapi, izaí).
